title: LaMelo Ball traded in NBA blockbuster: Why Timberwolves, Hornets made this big move
content:
In a surprising move, the Charlotte Hornets have a deal in place to trade LaMelo Ball, the franchise’s star point guard.

The Hornets are set to deal Ball and Josh Green to the Minnesota Timberwolves for Naz Reid, a 2033 first-round pick, three second-round picks and a series of first-round pick swaps, a league source confirmed to The Athletic.

Ball, 24, averaged 20.1 points and 7.1 assists in 2025-26, his fewest points per game since his rookie season, when he won the NBA’s Rookie of the Year award. He made the All-Star team the next season. That helped him earn a rookie max extension, with three years and approximately $130.7 million remaining. Reid, 26, a fan favorite in Minnesota, averaged 13.6 points and 6.2 rebounds this past season for the Timberwolves.

In addition to Reid and the unprotected 2033 first-rounder, the Hornets will receive the Wolves’ 2029, 2032 and 2033 second-round picks and first-round pick swaps in 2028, 2029 and 2030.

ESPN first reported the deal.

In the hours after this trade was agreed upon, there was elation running through the Wolves headquarters, team sources told The Athletic. They desperately needed a point guard and they went and got the one they believe fits them better than any other.

The Timberwolves have been pursuing Ball for the last two years, periodically checking in on his availability in hopes of pairing him with Edwards in a souped-up young backcourt. Finally, the Hornets started to show a willingness to move, and the Wolves went in aggressively to get a deal done.

President of basketball operations Tim Connelly and coach Chris Finch have long believed Ball is the perfect complement to Edwards, a superb passer and dynamic shooter who will open the floor for one of the best catch-and-shoot shooters in the league. They also believe that Ball will be much more helpful for Rudy Gobert on offense than any teammate he has had in Minnesota. The Wolves were woefully short of lob throwers, which is where Gobert does so much of his damage. Ball is one of the best in the league.

There are risks involved. Can Ball stay healthy? Is he mature enough to play deep into the playoffs? But the Wolves believe that putting him in a winning environment and allowing him to play wide open will benefit him and the rest of the team.

It also signals that the Wolves will pay the luxury tax in 2026-27. Prior to Ball’s arrival, the Wolves were looking to be a team that is under the tax. But this opportunity was too good for them to pass up. — Jon Krawczynski, Timberwolves senior writer

The trade is a significant shake-up for a Hornets team that has been on the upswing.

Charlotte finished 44-38 in the regular season, no small feat for a franchise that has had just one winning season over the last decade. They surged in the second half of the season to make the Eastern Conference’s Play-In Tournament, beating the Miami Heat in an overtime thriller thanks to Ball’s last-second layup. Charlotte was eliminated by the Orlando Magic three days later.

The decision to trade Ball, especially now, comes as a surprise.

The team has started to reframe itself around Brandon Miller, the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft, and Kon Knueppel, the narrow runner-up for rookie honors this past season, who averaged 18.5 points while hitting a rookie record 273 3s. With Ball gone, they’ll each get larger roles, as will Christian Anderson Jr., whom the Hornets took No. 18 in Tuesday’s draft.

The deal is the most audacious transaction yet by a relatively new front office that has made several astute, if smaller, choices so far. General manager Jeff Peterson was hired in the spring of 2024 and chose Charles Lee as the team’s head coach a few months later.

Now, they have made a deal large enough to push the franchise in a new direction under their guidance. Ball is gone, and the Hornets are moving on without a player long seen as the franchise’s pillar. — Mike Vorkunov, NBA staff writer

The inclusion of Reid in this trade is going to hurt Wolves fans for a long time.

Reid was a cult hero in Minnesota, captivating the fan base with his slick handle, his 3-point shooting and the sweat equity he devoted to changing his body and improving his game.

When Reid arrived in Minnesota as an undrafted free agent out of LSU in 2019, few knew what to make of the pudgy, but skilled big man. At the time, he looked to be too slow to be a wing and too small to be a center. But he lost more than 60 pounds and stayed in Minnesota every summer to work on his game and force his way onto the floor.

Eventually, a player who had no real position coming out of college could play three of them in the NBA. He spent time at power forward, center and small forward with the Wolves, adapting to different lineup combinations and dutifully waiting his turn behind Karl-Anthony Towns, Gobert and Randle.

Reid won the Sixth Man of the Year in 2024 and would eventually sign two lucrative contracts to stay in Minnesota — a three-year, $42 million deal in 2023 and a five-year, $125 million deal last summer.

Fans quickly fell for him, getting his name tattooed on their bodies during the Wolves’ conference finals run in 2024 and turning the Naz Reid beach towel giveaway into a flag that was flown all over the world. It became a symbol of the organization’s rise from the ashes.

Edwards was the only player who rivaled Reid’s popularity in the market, and fans will no doubt be crestfallen after it appeared that he would finally join the starting lineup when Randle was traded to Brooklyn.

But to get a player of Ball’s caliber, the Wolves had to part with real talent to do it. That is what Reid represents. Reid’s versatility and dynamic play gave the Wolves the final piece they needed to pry Ball away from the Hornets. — Krawczynski
